subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview:
The big idea of this unit is joyful and very hands-on: we can find things out, write them down, and then look at what we found. That is what it means to be a data collector. Nadia likes mango. Six children walked to school. When we ask a question and gather everyone's answers, we are collecting data.

First, you learn to record data using a form — a form is just a list of questions, and we write our answer next to each question. Forms can be on paper, or on a computer (an electronic form). Second, you learn to sort and group the data — put the same answers together — and to count each group, using tally marks and then a pictogram (a picture chart where one coloured box stands for one thing). Third, you learn to answer questions using what they made: How many? Which is the most (the favourite)? Which has the fewest?
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 1 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Say, in their own words, that data is the little bits of what we find out, and that a data collector finds things out and writes them down.
Record data by filling in a simple form (a list of questions), and know that a form can be on paper or on a computer.
Sort a small set of answers into groups (put the same ones together).
Count each group and use tally marks (one mark for one thing).
Make a simple pictogram by colouring one box for each thing.
Read a pictogram or a data table to answer questions — how many, which is the most (the favourite), and which has the fewest.
Enjoy being a data collector and take pride in the chart they made.

concepts.title: What is data? (unplugged)
concepts.explanation:
Data is the little bits of what we find out — answers, numbers, facts. A data collector asks a question, listens to the answers, and writes them down.

What is your favourite fruit — mango, banana, or dates? You are telling me data! I am writing it down — I am recording it.
concepts.example: Look — we collected all this data together! We are data collectors.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that your answer is a little bit of “data” that we are gathering and writing down? Can you answer the question with one clear choice?

concepts.title: Recording data with a form
concepts.explanation:
A form is a list of questions. Next to each question we write our answer — that is how we record data neatly, so we do not forget it. Some forms are on paper; some are on a computer.

Try it: You write or draw your name, tick or draw their favourite fruit, and colour their favourite colour.

Check yourself: Can you understand that a form holds questions, and we put our answers in? Can you fill in a simple form, with help — giving an answer to each question?
concepts.example: Find one real example of recording data with a form around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that a form holds questions, and we put our answers in? Can you fill in a simple form, with help — giving an answer to each question?

concepts.title: Sort, count, and tally (unplugged)
concepts.explanation:
When we have lots of data, we sort it — put the same answers together in groups. Then we count each group. A tally mark is a quick way to count: one little line for each thing.

One, two, three, four, five mango friends! Make three spots on the floor — one for mango, one for banana, one for dates — and try to sort themselves (or their cards) into the right group.
concepts.example: Do it yourself: sort, count, and tally. Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you count a small group (up to five) and match the right number to it? Can you see a tally mark as one-for-one? Can you put the same items into one group?

concepts.title: Make a pictogram and answer questions (unplugged)
concepts.explanation:
A pictogram is a picture chart. One box (or one picture) stands for one thing. A pictogram lets us see the data at a glance. Once we can see it, we can answer questions: How many? Which is the most — the favourite? Which has the fewest?

Using the numbers from Session 3, colour one box for you: five boxes for mango, three for banana, two for dates.
concepts.example: Do it yourself: make a pictogram and answer questions. Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you colour the right number of boxes (one box per child)?

concepts.title: Be a data collector: the Mini-Project
concepts.explanation:
They help Nadia be a data collector: ask a few friends their favourite fruit, record each answer with a tally mark, count the tallies, colour a pictogram, and then answer which fruit is the favourite.

What is your favourite fruit? Then count the marks and colour the pictogram together.
concepts.example: Now you can (or pair) go and collect a small sample — about five friends is plenty. Show the Mini-Project sheet.
concepts.checkYourself: Does your pictogram match your tallies? Does you collect and record real answers with tally marks?

debugging.symptom: Data is a hard word only computers have.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: Not at all. Data is just what we find out. Your favourite fruit is data. Where you sit is data. We collect data all day long.

debugging.symptom: I do not need to write it down — I will remember.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: We forget! That is why a data collector records the data straight away, with a mark or on a form, so none of it is lost.

debugging.symptom: One box can stand for the whole group.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: In a pictogram, one box means one thing. One box, one child. If five you like mango, we colour five boxes, not one.

debugging.symptom: The shortest row is the most.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: It is the other way round. The longest coloured row is the most (the favourite); the shortest is the fewest. Count them together to be sure.

debugging.symptom: I must ask everybody in the whole school.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: No. A data collector can ask just a small group — five friends is plenty for us. We only count the answers we actually collected.

debugging.symptom: The pictogram and the table are different data.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: They show the same data in two ways — one with coloured boxes, one with numbers. Mango is five boxes and also the number 5.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

project.brief: Bring together everything from Be a Data Collector into one finished piece of work you can show and explain.
steps: Plan first: write down what your be a data collector project has to do before you build anything.
Build the smallest version that does one of those things, and run it.
Add one feature at a time, testing after each one.
When something breaks, change one thing, run it again, and note what fixed it.
Check your work against every success criterion below before you call it finished.
successCriteria: I asked my friends the question.
I made a tally mark for each answer.
I counted the marks and wrote the number.

selfAssessment: I can say, in their own words, that data is the little bits of what we find out, and that a data collector finds things out and writes them down.
I can record data by filling in a simple form (a list of questions), and know that a form can be on paper or on a computer.
I can sort a small set of answers into groups (put the same ones together).
I can count each group and use tally marks (one mark for one thing).
I can make a simple pictogram by colouring one box for each thing.
I can read a pictogram or a data table to answer questions — how many, which is the most (the favourite), and which has the fewest.
I can enjoy being a data collector and take pride in the chart they made.
